memoryText: Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Isaiah 7:14 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Ahaz, king of Judah, was afraid. Two armies were marching against him, and Isaiah met him with an offer: ask for any sign you like, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven. Ahaz refused with a pious-sounding excuse. He had already decided to trust Assyria instead of God. So the Lord gave a sign anyway.

“The Lord himself will give you a sign.” It is a gift that is given whether or not it is asked for. Grace often works like that. God gives more than we ask and sometimes more than we deserve.

“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” In Isaiah’s time, a young woman would bear a child, and before he was old enough to know right from wrong, the threat from the northern kings would be gone. Matthew, writing under the Spirit’s guidance, sees a deeper meaning. The sign finds its full meaning in Mary and the birth of Jesus, born of a virgin.

“And shall call his name Immanuel.” The name means “God with us.” It is the whole message of the gospel in two words. God has not stayed at a distance. He has come near, in flesh, in the middle of our fear and trouble. Ahaz needed to know that God was with him. We need to know it too.

Say this verse when you are afraid. The promise is not that every threat will vanish, but that God is with you. In Christ, the one who is called Immanuel has promised, “I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
weekInReview: This week you began the unit that surrounds the Assyrian crisis. You read of Hezekiah’s trust in the LORD when Sennacherib’s army stood outside Jerusalem, and of his later pride when he showed the Babylonian envoys his treasures. You entered the book of Isaiah, with the courtroom scene of chapter 1 and its great invitation, “Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.” You read the song of the vineyard, in which God looked for justice and found bloodshed, and you prayed Psalms 80 and 81 for the vine to be restored and for the people to listen. And you stood in the temple with Isaiah, saw the Holy One high and lifted up, heard the cry of “Holy, holy, holy,” and received the sign of Immanuel. The week taught that God is holy, that he provides his own cleansing, and that he is with his people.
reflectionQuestions: Isaiah saw God’s holiness and was undone, then cleansed, then sent. Where are you in that pattern right now?
Jesus is the true vine who bears the fruit Israel never did. What would it look like to abide in him this week?
Immanuel means “God with us.” Where do you most need to remember that he is with you right now?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for Immanuel, God with us.
Ask him to cleanse you, send you, and be with you.
